idiom_name: abstract class with a (sealed) template method + protected abstract steps and protected virtual hooks
implementation_notes: C# gives the pattern directly: an abstract base class carries the skeleton, `protected abstract` members are the required steps, `protected virtual` members are hooks with default bodies (often empty), and the skeleton is non-virtual by default - mark it `sealed` when it overrides a virtual from a further base. Concrete classes override with `override`, and `sealed override` can close a step at a specific level. The framework convention is exactly this shape: an ASP.NET controller action or a hosted service implementing BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync supplies only the steps, while the base class owns the request pipeline, lifetime and cancellation wiring. Reach for the interface variant when no instance state or constructor is needed.
pitfalls: A hook that throws NotImplementedException from a virtual body is a contract smell: either make the step abstract so the compiler forces it, or give it a real default.
An async skeleton must pass the CancellationToken into every step and await it; a step that ignores the token stalls the whole flow, and an `async void` hook cannot be awaited at all.
Calling a virtual step from the constructor runs before the derived field initialisers, and exposing a step as `public virtual` re-opens it to direct calls from outside the hierarchy.

variants.name: Default interface method as the skeleton (C# 8)
variants.implementation_notes: Since C# 8 an interface method may have a body, so the skeleton itself can live on an interface: Generate() calls FetchData/AnalyzeData/ExportReport, implementors supply the steps, and the API author can later add steps with defaults without breaking existing implementors - the motivation Microsoft documents for the feature ("virtual extension methods", interoperating with Java default methods and Swift protocol extensions). It replaces the abstract base class wherever no instance state or constructor is needed; the interface cannot hold state, and because the skeleton is an ordinary interface method any implementor may override it, so keep an abstract class when the sequence must be sealed.
variants.idiom_name: interface with a default method carrying the skeleton over required members
pitfalls: The skeleton cannot be sealed in an interface, so any implementor may restate Generate() and discard the sequence - use an abstract class when the order must hold.
Interfaces have no instance state and no constructors, so steps that need shared fields must be refactored into an abstract class or passed in explicitly.
A type that implements two interfaces with the same default member must override it explicitly to resolve the ambiguity, exactly as in Java.
